title: Turkey Oak: Ancient Turkey Oaks You Can Visit
meta_description: A fast, tall Balkan oak planted on purpose: Genoa's reaches 41 metres, taller than the redwood beside it; Utrecht counts four as one register entry.
intro: Quercus cerris is native to southeastern Europe and Asia Minor, and every planting mapped here happened on purpose: gardeners liked how fast it grows and how large it gets while the person who planted it is still around to see it. Genoa's, in the English-style grounds of Villa Serra above the city, is the surprise: 41 metres, taller than the Californian redwood sixty metres away, a height this oak rarely reaches in its own range. Caserta's grows in the royal park's English Garden among trees collected from Australia and California, thirty-five metres and about 150 years old. Utrecht's four stand together on an old city-wall bastion, close enough that the Dutch register counts them as one entry rather than four, two planted around 1835 and two around 1870. The leaves give it away: stiffer and more deeply cut than a pedunculate oak's, with whiskery bud scales and mossy, curl-wrapped acorn cups.
